results.summary: Keep this as the Obstruction Point line over Grand Pass, Cameron Pass and Lost Pass (the line its trailhead, road, permits, waypoints, itinerary and exit already describe), and rewrite the approach, descent, beta and route-breakdown text that described a wrong-way shortcut from Grand Pass or the Dosewallips/Hayden Pass line.
results.evidence: The Dosewallips road to the Hayden Pass line has been washed out since 2002, adding a long road walk, while the row's trailhead card, road, access, pins, itinerary, timing and descent all already follow the Obstruction Point line. Two backpacking reports describe the trail from Obstruction Point over Grand Pass, down into Cameron Basin, steeply over Cameron Pass and on to Lost Pass (one camped at Upper Cameron at 10.4 mi, another reached Lost Pass at 12.5 mi); the steep path from Dose Meadows to Lost Pass is under a mile. Lost Pass (47.807,-123.342) lies about 1.4 mi east-northeast of Claywood's summit (47.801,-123.370), and a high-route report links Lost Pass to Claywood off-trail. The easiest route is rated class 2, and an ascent log records a brief class 3 stretch on the west side of the summit. The old approach text sent parties cross-country east-northeast from Grand Pass, but the peak lies about 5 mi south of Grand Pass. Not changed (only one source each, so left as they are): the itinerary's day-1 7 mi and 21.5 mi round-trip figures, and the Cameron Pass pin's 7.6 mi, all look short against the 10.4-12.5 mi those reports give to Upper Cameron and Lost Pass.

ops.expect: From the Obstruction Point Trailhead (6,150 ft) — reached via the narrow, unpaved Obstruction Point Road that branches off Hurricane Ridge Road just below Hurricane Ridge — follow the Grand Pass Trail as it climbs onto and traverses Lillian Ridge. The first mile-plus is an easy, open ridge walk (the unmarked boot path up the Lillian Ridge Way / Elk Mountain high route splits off here for those doing the ridge-top variation instead). The trail then drops into the Grand Lake basin before climbing steadily to Grand Pass (6,488 ft) at roughly 5.95 mi and only a few hundred feet of net gain from the trailhead but close to 2,000 ft of total climbing, because the trail first loses well over 1,000 ft into the lake basin. Seasonal tarns in the Grand Lake basin below the pass are the last reliable water before the climb to the pass — fill up there, since water on the open ridge is unreliable. From Grand Pass the maintained trail ends for this objective: the route to Claywood's summit continues cross-country, dropping a few hundred feet down loose scree and shale on the pass's east side into the upper Cameron Creek/Lillian Basin drainage (moderately steep and loose underfoot, worse when wet — this gully is the one approach-specific hazard called out by parties doing this same descent off Grand Pass in trip reports). From the basin floor, contour and climb generally east-northeast across open alpine benches and talus toward the Cameron–Claywood divide, staying below Mount Cameron's north ridge and aiming for the shoulder immediately west/southwest of Claywood's summit block (Claywood's nearest higher neighbor, Mount Cameron, sits about 2.4 mi northeast; Mt. Fromme and Sentinel Peak are just southeast of Claywood in the same cluster). The final several hundred feet to the 6,836 ft summit are class 2–3 scrambling on broken shale and loose scree — similar in character to the well-documented scramble route on neighboring Lost Peak in the same basin system. This whole cross-country stretch beyond Grand Pass (roughly 4–5 mi round trip of the route's total ~21.5 mi) is unmarked, off-trail, and route-finding is real: bring a topo/GPS track and only attempt it with good visibility, since the terrain is used almost exclusively by peak-baggers linking Claywood with Cameron, Fromme, Lost, and Sentinel rather than by any constructed path.
ops.value: From the Obstruction Point Trailhead (6,150 ft), reached by the narrow, unpaved Obstruction Point Road that leaves Hurricane Ridge Road just below Hurricane Ridge, follow the Grand Pass Trail along open Lillian Ridge, then down into Grand Valley past Grand and Moose Lakes and up past Gladys Lake to Grand Pass (6,488 ft) at about 6 miles. Net gain to the pass is only a few hundred feet, but the trail first loses well over 1,000 ft into the valley, so total climbing to the pass is close to 2,000 ft. Beyond Grand Pass the trail drops steeply into Cameron Basin, then climbs steeply to Cameron Pass (6,448 ft), the highest trail-served pass in the park; the last part of that climb is loose and rocky in spots and holds snow into midsummer. From Cameron Pass the primitive trail descends into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River and continues to Lost Pass (5,570 ft), the low notch between Lost Peak and Claywood. Parties camp in Upper Cameron Basin or in Lost Basin and climb the peak from there. At Lost Pass leave the trail and head west-southwest across open heather benches and talus toward Claywood, the higher, greyer and more broken summit about a mile and a half away. The final several hundred feet are class 2-3 scrambling on broken shale and loose scree, with a short class 3 step on the west side of the summit block. Everything beyond Lost Pass is unmarked and off-trail, so carry a map and GPS and go only in good visibility.

ops.expect: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved. From the summit, reverse the class 2–3 scramble down to the shoulder on the Cameron–Claywood divide, then descend back into the upper Cameron Creek/Lillian Basin drainage on the same talus and open benches used on the way up. Regain Grand Pass by climbing the loose scree/shale slope on the basin's west side; this slope is notably looser and more insecure on the reascent than it felt going down, so expect slow, careful travel with some hand use, and glissadeable snow patches here in early season instead. From Grand Pass, follow the Grand Pass Trail back over Lillian Ridge to the Obstruction Point Trailhead. Watch for afternoon thunderstorm buildup over the exposed ridge on the final miles, and budget real time for the cross-country middle section in both directions — at roughly 21.5 mi / 34.6 km round trip with a significant off-trail component, this is a trip built around a basin camp rather than a single day, and parties should reverse-navigate carefully rather than assume the outbound track is easy to retrace.
ops.value: This is a walk-off and downclimb; no rappels are needed. Reverse the class 2-3 scramble carefully on the loose shale, then return east-northeast over the talus and heather benches to Lost Pass and back to camp. To exit, climb out of Lost Basin to Cameron Pass, descend steeply into Cameron Basin, climb back over Grand Pass and follow the Grand Pass Trail through Grand Valley and along Lillian Ridge to Obstruction Point. The loose, steep ground on both sides of Cameron Pass is slower than it looks, and snow can linger there early in the season. Watch for afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge on the final miles. This is a multi-day trip built around a basin camp, not a single day.

ops.expect: Claywood has no maintained summit trail. Parties approach via the Dosewallips River Trail to Dose Meadows, then climb the short but very steep unmaintained path to Lost Pass (5,570 ft) on the ridge between Lost Peak and Claywood, and finally leave the trail entirely for a cross-country scramble over talus, heather benches, and loose rock to the 6,836 ft summit. It is almost always combined with neighboring Lost Peak, Mount Fromme, and/or Sentinel Peak from a single Dose Meadows or Lost Pass camp, since the approach itself is a multi-day undertaking.
ops.value: Claywood has no maintained summit trail. This line starts at Obstruction Point and follows the Grand Pass Trail over Grand Pass, down into Cameron Basin and steeply up over Cameron Pass, then drops into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River below Lost Pass. From Lost Pass (5,570 ft) the route leaves the trail and heads west-southwest over heather benches, talus and loose shale to the 6,836 ft summit. It is often combined with Lost Peak, Mount Fromme or Sentinel Peak from the same camp. The southern way in, a long valley walk up the Dosewallips to Dose Meadows and then the short, very steep path to Lost Pass, reaches the same pass.

results.summary: Keep this as the Meade Glacier route its name, face, gear and season advice already describe, and rewrite the approach, overview, beta, descent, route breakdown and approach card that described the separate Klickton Divide ridge walk or the Conrad Glacier line.
results.evidence: Two route descriptions give the Meade Glacier line from Conrad Meadows: Trail #1120 and the Surprise Lake loop (right fork to its high point), cross-country west into a basin, a short drop to the foot of the Meade, up the glacier (now a series of snowfields) right of the rock band splitting it, to the ridge, then a goat/boot path on the southwest side to a saddle and a short class 2-3 scramble to the summit just west of it. Neither mentions Klickton Divide. The Klickton Divide line (from Warm Lake southwest to the divide, then northwest along the crest) is a separate ridge route with no glacier travel. The Conrad Glacier alternative in the old beta is already its own sibling row. Gilbert Peak's Meade Glacier lies on its southeast slopes, matching the row's SE aspect.

ops.expect: The standard/easiest ascent: a long approach through Conrad Meadows and over Klickton Divide, gaining the Meade Glacier's permanent snowfields on the peak's southeast side and finishing with a short class 3 scramble to the summit block.
ops.value: The standard, most straightforward ascent: a long approach through Conrad Meadows and up the Surprise Lake loop trail, then cross-country to the foot of the Meade Glacier on the peak's southeast side, up its snowfields to the ridge, and a short class 3 scramble to the summit.

ops.expect: From the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead, follow Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows and up toward Warm Lake, then traverse southwest to Klickton Divide and follow the ridge (mixing snow and rock, with Gilbert in view most of the way) toward the summit block. Alternatively, climbers can cross the east side of the Conrad Glacier to the saddle east of the summit, drop onto the Meade Glacier, and climb it (now largely reduced to persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier) to a rock outcrop below the final pitch. Either way, the route tops out with a steep snow/scree slope and a short, loose class 3 scramble through a notch to the true summit. Very popular and rated the most straightforward line up the peak, though it is a long day (~20 miles round trip) with real elevation gain.
ops.value: From the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead, follow Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows to the Surprise Lake loop and take its right fork to the trail's high point. Leave the trail there, climb west into a basin, cross it left of some large mounds and drop briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier. Climb the glacier (now largely a series of persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier) near the center of the cirque, right of the rock band that splits the upper and lower sections, then right of the snow dome to gain the ridge. A rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to a small saddle just east of the true summit, and a short, loose class 3 scramble finishes it. Popular and the most straightforward line up the peak, though it is a long outing (~20 miles round trip) with real elevation gain.

expect.name: Conrad Meadows and the South Fork Tieton to Klickton Divide
expect.notes:
Drive to the Conrad Meadows and South Fork Tieton trailhead at road's end, about 4,044 ft, reached by the Tieton Reservoir road and then the South Fork Tieton road off the highway west of Naches. The last several miles are gravel.

Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows, crossing Conrad Creek, into the Goat Rocks Wilderness and on toward Surprise Lake and Warm Lake. From there climb southwest to gain Klickton Divide near Point 6,882, then follow the ridge northwest toward the summit, mixing snow and rock with Gilbert in view most of the way.

An alternative from the same trailhead crosses the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle east of the summit, drops onto the Meade, and climbs it — now largely persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier — to a rock outcrop below the final pitch.

This is a long day: roughly 20 miles round trip with real gain, and limited water late in a dry season.
hazards: A steep summit snowfield requiring solid self-arrest
Loose rock on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk between parties climbing close together
Receding glaciers that can still hide crevasses and moats early season
A long, remote round trip of roughly 20 miles with limited water in a dry year
Ridge navigation that depends on visibility once off the trail
expect.baseFinding:
GAINING KLICKTON DIVIDE IN THE RIGHT PLACE IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM, AND EVERYTHING BEFORE IT IS TRAIL.

You leave the trail beyond Warm Lake and climb SOUTHWEST to gain the divide near POINT 6,882. From there the ridge runs NORTHWEST to the peak. Two directions, in that order: southwest to gain, northwest to follow. Getting the second one wrong walks you away from the mountain along the same ridge.

THE POSITIVE THAT MAKES THIS A GENEROUS ROUTE IN CLEAR WEATHER, AND A HARSH ONE IN CLOUD: once you are on the divide, GILBERT IS IN VIEW ALMOST THE WHOLE WAY. If you cannot see the peak from the ridge you are either not on the divide or the day has closed in, and in the second case the ridge crest itself is the handrail.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS A NOTCH, AND THERE IS ONLY ONE. The route tops out with a steep snow and scree slope and then a SHORT, LOOSE CLASS 3 SCRAMBLE THROUGH A NOTCH to the true summit. Short is the operative word: the summit is immediately above the notch. If you have gone through a gap and the ground keeps rising well beyond it, you are at the wrong gap.

THE NEGATIVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM ITS SIBLING ON THE SAME PEAK: this line goes ONTO THE RIDGE. The other route from this trailhead goes UNDER the peak — across the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle, then onto the Meade. If you find yourself roping up for glacier travel before you have been on a ridge, you are on that one instead.

SELF-ARREST IS PART OF THE BASE FINDING HERE, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the snowfield below the summit is steep enough that the route assumes you can hold a slip on it. Arriving without an axe is a reason to turn round at the divide.

Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin. Cross it left of some large mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

This is a long day: roughly 20 miles round trip with real gain, and limited water late in a dry season.
hazards: A steep snowfield below the summit requiring solid self-arrest
Loose rock on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk between parties climbing close together

value.baseFinding:
LEAVING THE TRAIL IN THE RIGHT PLACE AND FINDING THE FOOT OF THE MEADE IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM, AND EVERYTHING BEFORE IT IS TRAIL.

Take the RIGHT fork of the Surprise Lake loop and stay on it to its HIGH POINT. From there climb WEST into a basin, cross it keeping LEFT of the large mounds, and drop a short way to the foot of the glacier. If you are climbing onto a long ridge crest before you have reached any snow, you are on the ridge line to the south, not this route.

ON THE GLACIER, ONE ROCK BAND ORGANISES EVERYTHING. It splits the lower glacier from the upper; go up near the center of the cirque and pass it on its RIGHT. Above it, stay right of the snow dome and the ridge comes easily.

THE BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE IS A SMALL SADDLE, AND THE SUMMIT IS JUST WEST OF IT. From the ridge a rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to that saddle; the true summit is immediately to its west, a short, loose class 3 scramble. If the ground keeps rising well beyond a gap, you are at the wrong gap.

THE NEGATIVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM ITS SIBLING ON THE SAME PEAK: this line reaches the Meade from BELOW, out of the basin. The other route from this trailhead crosses the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle east of the summit and drops onto the Meade from above. If you are on the Conrad Glacier, you are on that one instead.

SELF-ARREST IS PART OF THE BASE FINDING HERE, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the snowfield below the summit is steep enough that the route assumes you can hold a slip on it. Arriving without an axe is a reason to turn round at the foot of the glacier.

results.summary: Keep this as Pernod's original 1952 line (from the east side up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti, then the northeast corner) and rewrite the approach, pitch table, day plan, summit note and rappel notes that had been copied from the separate West Face and South Face routes; the beta no longer credits a guidebook.
results.evidence: The 1952 first-ascent account has the party climbing from the east (Silver Star Creek side) over moraine and ice to the eastern walls and the notch between Pernod and Chianti, with the first lead to a ledge on the northeast corner, a bolt for an insecure section, an 8-foot bolt-assisted pendulum around an overhanging corner, summit bolts placed from a shoulder stand, and rappels to the notch then long rappels to the glacier. A later ascent account from a Burgundy Col camp approached from the east side, climbed obliquely up and around to the north notch between Pernod and Chianti (about three pitches, mostly 4th and 5th class) and descended by rappel on double ropes; the same writer rates the climbing moderate 5.5-5.7 and not sustained. The route database lists only the Direct West Face (reached by the gully contouring right from the bench) and the South Face (5.9 A0, rappelling to the Chablis notch) on Pernod; both are separate sibling rows, and those were the sources of this row's approach, pitch table, itinerary and rappel table. Numbers not changed for want of a second source: pitches 6, length_m 213, gain/loss 4,000, the Grade III / III-IV commitment, and the 5.5-5.7 rock grade (one source only).

ops.expect: Per Beckey-guide-derived route descriptions, Pernod and neighboring Chablis are considered the easiest of the Wine Spires and can be climbed in an easy day; the climbing is moderate (5.5-5.7) and not sustained.
ops.value: Pernod and neighboring Chablis are the easiest of the Wine Spires, and this line is a reasonable day from a Burgundy Col camp. The climbing is moderate (about 5.5-5.7) and not sustained. It climbs from the east side up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti and then up the northeast corner to a tiny summit block; the South Face and the Direct West Face are separate, harder routes on the same spire.

ops.find: From the bench, leave the main Burgundy Col trail and contour right past a couple of subsidiary buttresses, dropping slightly before regaining a large talus/scree gully that runs directly to the base of Pernod's west face. This final gully is loose scree-over-slab ('kitty litter,' Class 2-3) and is the route-finding and footing crux of the approach, especially under a pack — trekking poles help. All told the approach is roughly 3,500-4,000 ft of gain over about 3 miles one-way (3-5 hours for a fit party). Lingering snow in the gully into early July may require an axe/light traction for the last few hundred feet in a big-snow year; check current conditions before committing. Burgundy Col itself also holds 3-4 bivy sites (one large enough for a 2-person tent), with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing.
ops.replace: From the bench, continue up the main climbers' trail over steep talus and scree to Burgundy Col, which holds three or four bivy sites with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties. From the col, cross to the east side and traverse south over snow and talus at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin, below the east walls of Chianti and Pernod. From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to the notch between Chianti and Pernod; this section runs to roughly three pitches of mostly 4th and 5th class. Lingering snow on the east side into early July may call for an axe and light traction.

expect.name: The Wine Spires pullout and the bench camp, then contour right off the Burgundy Col trail into the gully under the west face
expect.notes: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, directly across the highway from the Wine Spires, a boot and climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop, and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The creek can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt. The trail gains steeply and steadily, on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles, to a broad flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps. THIS BENCH IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER: small tarns and a creek trickle that can run dry by late summer. Roughly 3,500-4,000 ft of gain over about 3 miles one-way, 3-5 hours for a fit party. Note that the aspect recorded for this route says north while its own approach and descent describe the west face and an east-side rappel.
hazards: Loose scree-over-slab in the final approach gully, the footing crux of the day
Lingering snow in the gully into early July in a big-snow year
A rappel descent down the opposite side of the peak onto a glacier, followed by a re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Natural anchors only, with aging fixed webbing; carry cord to back up or replace
A single 60 m rope is tight in places on the descent; many parties run a 70 m or doubles
The bench is the last reliable water and can run dry by late summer
expect.baseFinding:
LEAVE THE MAIN BURGUNDY COL TRAIL AT THE BENCH. THAT IS THE TURN, AND MISSING IT IS THE ONLY WAY TO GET THIS APPROACH WRONG. From the bench, contour RIGHT past a couple of subsidiary buttresses, DROPPING SLIGHTLY before regaining a large talus and scree gully that runs directly to the base of Pernod's west face.

SO THERE IS A SMALL DESCENT IN THE MIDDLE OF AN OTHERWISE RELENTLESS CLIMB, AND THAT DIP IS THE CONFIRMATION. If everything you have done since the bench has been uphill, you are still on the Burgundy Col trail.

THE GULLY IS THE ROUTE-FINDING AND FOOTING CRUX OF THE APPROACH: loose scree over slab, class 2-3, described as kitty litter, especially under a pack. Trekking poles help. Lingering snow in it into early July may require an axe or light traction for the last few hundred feet in a big-snow year.

ARRIVAL: the base of Pernod's west face, THE TALLEST WALL IN THE WINE SPIRES. Six pitches at Grade III. If the wall above you is one of the smaller buttresses you passed on the contour, you stopped too early.

AND FOR PARTIES WHO CAMP HIGH INSTEAD: Burgundy Col itself holds three or four bivy sites, one large enough for a two-person tent, with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing. Those shelters are a positive identification of the col.

DESCENT IS BY RAPPEL DOWN THE BACK, NOT BY REVERSING THE APPROACH GULLY: the first rappel drops into the notch just below and east of the top, then a string of rappels continues down the peak's EAST side into the Silver Star Glacier basin, on the order of four to five in total. Anchors are natural, slung horns and blocks with occasional aging fixed webbing, not bolts. Once on the glacier, climb back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the standard climbers' trail.

value.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then across the east side to the Pernod–Chianti notch
value.notes: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, directly across the highway from the Wine Spires, a boot and climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop, and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The creek can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt. The trail gains steeply and steadily, on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles, to a broad flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps. THIS BENCH IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER: small tarns and a creek trickle that can run dry by late summer. Above it the trail climbs steep talus and scree to Burgundy Col, the usual camp for this climb. From the col the route crosses to the east side of the spires and traverses south below their east walls to reach the notch between Chianti and Pernod.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the climb to Burgundy Col
Snow and névé at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin on the east side, with moats along the rock late in the season
Roughly three pitches of mostly 4th and 5th class to reach the notch
A rappel descent back down the east side, followed by a re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Old first-ascent bolts on the summit block; carry cord to back up or replace old slings
The bench is the last reliable water and can run dry by late summer
value.baseFinding:
THIS LINE IS CLIMBED FROM THE EAST, NOT FROM THE WEST FACE GULLY. Stay on the main climbers' trail past the bench all the way to Burgundy Col; the gully that contours right off the bench leads to the base of the west face, which is the start of a different and much harder route.

FROM THE COL, CROSS TO THE EAST SIDE AND GO SOUTH. Traverse below the east walls of Chianti and then Pernod, on snow and talus at the edge of the glacier basin. Pernod is the highest of the four spires and sits just south of Chianti.

THE KEY FEATURE IS THE NOTCH BETWEEN CHIANTI AND PERNOD. From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to that notch; the ground is mostly 4th and 5th class, roughly three pitches. Going south from the col you pass below Chianti first, and the notch you want is the one immediately south of it. The next notch beyond Pernod separates Pernod from Chablis and is the wrong one.

FROM THE NOTCH THE ROUTE GOES UP THE NORTHEAST CORNER to the small summit block, which carries old first-ascent bolts that are worth backing up.

FOR PARTIES WHO CAMP HIGH: Burgundy Col holds three or four bivy sites, one large enough for a two-person tent, with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing. Those shelters are a positive identification of the col.

DESCENT IS BY RAPPEL: back to the notch, then long rappels down the east side to the snow at the edge of the glacier basin. From there climb back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' trail.

expect.notes: Lower-angle rock gains the base of the technical climbing above the scree gully approach; easy ground used to reach the first real belay stance on the wall.
Moderate crack and corner climbing following essentially the same line the 1952 first-ascent party (Beckey, Wilde, McGowan) established, before the angle and difficulty pick up higher on the face.
Sustained face moves lead toward the route's historically hardest section; solid granite with adequate but spaced protection.
The insecure section the first-ascent party protected with a hand-drilled Rawl-drive bolt — the old fixed bolt (or its replacement) still marks the technical crux of the lower wall.

Passes the overhanging, holdless corner that stumped the 1952 first ascensionists, who bolted and pendulumed roughly 8 feet around it on aid; most modern parties free it near 5.9, though a short pull on gear (A0) remains an option if it doesn't go free.

Finishes at the small summit block using bolts the first-ascent trio placed from a shoulder-stand to reach the top; treat these old, weathered bolts with caution and back them up with gear/slings where possible before starting the multi-rappel descent.
expect.anchor: Old fixed bolts (summit, FA shoulder-stand aid points)

value.pitch: East side to the Pernod–Chianti notch
value.notes: From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to the notch between Pernod and Chianti; roughly three pitches, mostly 4th and 5th class.

From the notch the line goes up the northeast corner. The first-ascent party used aid, a bolt to protect an insecure section and a bolt for an 8-foot pendulum around an overhanging corner, and reached the small summit block with bolts placed from a shoulder stand; the old fixed bolts are worth inspecting and backing up.

ops.expect: This is a rappel descent, not a walk-off. From the summit, the first rappel drops into the notch just below/east of the top — anchors on this line are natural (slung horns and blocks, occasional aging fixed webbing/tat) rather than bolted, so carry some cord to back up or replace sun-bleached slings. From the notch, continue down a further string of rappels on the peak's back (east) side into the Silver Star Glacier basin rather than reversing the approach gully; expect on the order of 4-5 rappels total to reach easy glacier snow/talus. A single 60m rope works but is tight in a few spots — many parties run a 70m single or rappel on doubled ropes so they're not left short above the next anchor — and watch for rope-stuck hazard pulling ropes through the blocky terrain. Once down on the Silver Star Glacier, climb/traverse back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the standard climbers' trail (scree bench, then timbered rib) back to the SR-20 pullout, essentially reversing the approach. Rope up for the glacier crossing if there's any question about moat/crevasse conditions, and budget real time for the loose 'kitty litter' scree below the col — it's notoriously slow going.
ops.value: This is a rappel descent, not a walk-off. Rappel from the summit block back to the notch between Pernod and Chianti, then make long rappels down the east side to the snow and névé at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin. No rappel count is published for this line; carry double ropes, and cord to back up or replace old slings and bolts. From the glacier edge, traverse back north below Chianti and climb a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' trail (scree, the bench, then the timbered rib) to the SR-20 pullout. Watch for moats along the rock late in the season, and budget real time for the loose scree below the col.

expect.notes: Rappel from Pernod's true summit down the south face to a notch/ledge near Chablis Spire; a single 70m rope reaches, a 60m leaves you short of the notch.

results.summary: Keep this as the south-side snow gully reached from the col southeast of the summit, and replace the pitch table, 50-degree angle, ice grade, pitch count and length, gear notes and day plan that had been copied from a different crux on the 2007 range traverse.
results.evidence: The 2007 traverse account places its 40 m of 4th-class rock, 100+ m of 50-degree ice and 100+ m of rappelling on the crossing near South Twin, not on Little Sister, where the South Couloir was simply skied on day two. The 2015 winter ascent page (two party members' accounts) describes hard snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit, a steep last bit of snow to the col, a traverse onto the south aspect and a snow and rock slope/gully rated 3rd class, climbed unroped, with a bit of mixed climbing near the summit on reasonably solid rock; a double-60 m rappel from near the top and another from the col; about 10 mi, ~5,000 ft and 12 hours car to car. No source gives this gully an angle, an ice grade, a pitch count or a length, so max_angle, ice_grade, pitches and length_m are cleared rather than replaced. Discipline stays 'ice' (a snow/mixed gully), though 'mountaineering' may suit it better; not changed.

ops.expect: A steep snow/ice/mixed couloir on Little Sister's south side, called out in a 2007 account of the first known ski traverse of the entire Twin Sisters Range as 'the proudest line of the trip.'
ops.value: A snow and rock gully on Little Sister's south side, reached by climbing to the col southeast of the summit and traversing onto the south aspect. It has been skied during a traverse of the whole Twin Sisters Range and climbed in winter as a moderate snow gully with a bit of mixed ground near the summit.

expect.notes: About 40 m of fourth-class rock forms the entry to the line, per the published description of the Twin Sister High Route. On the ski descent this section was protected and rappelled. Depending on snow year this can be buried, in which case it climbs as moderate snow.

First rope length of the 100+ m of 50-degree ice and mixed rock described in the published account. A winter party climbed this ground unroped in firm conditions, describing it as a snow-and-rock slope/gully. Screws where there is real ice; often only snow over rock.

Second rope length, finishing with a bit of mixed climbing on reasonably solid rock near the summit; third-class scrambling on the final sections. The 100+ m section is split here into two rope lengths for planning — it is a continuous 100+ m, not discrete pitches.

value.notes: The last snow up to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit is steep. In hard winter conditions it cramponed well on the way up but was judged too sketchy to downclimb on single axes, so it was rappelled on the way down.

Traverse from the col onto the south side and climb a snow and rock slope/gully, with a bit of mixed climbing on reasonably solid rock near the summit. A winter party climbed it unroped in good snow; it softens as the south aspect warms.

ops.expect: Light alpine kit rather than a rock rack. One 60 m rope is enough for the documented rappels (Abegg's party carried two 60 m ropes and used them for a single double-rope rappel from near the top, and noted one rope would have sufficed at the col). Bring 2-3 ice screws for the 50-degree ice, a picket or two for snow anchors, a small selection of nuts and slings for rock anchors on the fourth-class band and summit mixed ground, and a generous amount of cord/webbing plus rap rings — there are no reliable fixed anchors and you should plan to leave gear. One technical ice tool plus a mountaineering axe is a reasonable compromise for AI1 mixed ground; Abegg's party used single axes.
ops.value: Light alpine kit rather than a rock rack. One 60 m rope is enough for the documented rappels: a winter party carried two 60 m ropes, used them together for one rappel from near the top, and found a single rope would have done at the col. Bring a picket or two for snow anchors, a few nuts and slings for rock anchors on the mixed ground near the summit, and plenty of cord or webbing plus rap rings; there are no reliable fixed anchors, so plan to leave gear. A mountaineering axe each is the usual tool, and the winter ascent was made on single axes.

ops.expect: Protection is thin and improvised. The 50-degree ice takes screws when it is real ice and takes nothing when it is unconsolidated snow over rock, which is the more common case. The fourth-class rock band and the mixed summit ground offer occasional horns, blocks and small nut placements in the dunite, which is coarse and generally solid but is not a splitter-crack medium. Plan on running it out on moderate snow and saving your gear for anchors. Because you will rappel the line, budget cord and rings for two stations you may have to build from scratch.
ops.value: Protection is thin and improvised. The south-side gully is snow and rock, climbed unroped in good conditions, with a bit of mixed ground near the summit where the dunite offers occasional horns, blocks and small nut placements; it is coarse and generally solid but is not a splitter-crack medium. Expect to move unroped or run it out on moderate snow and save your gear for anchors. Because you will rappel, budget cord and rings for two stations you may have to build from scratch.

ops.expect: Part of a 3-day, ~26-mile south-to-north ski traverse of the whole range (Step Sister, Last Sister, Saddle Slab, Nancy, Barbara, Trisolace, Cinderella, Little Sister, Hayden, Skookum, South Twin, North Twin, and an unnamed peak called Mirage), with roughly 12,000 ft gained and 14,000 ft lost overall — not just on Little Sister.
ops.value: A long single day from the Elbow Lake Trailhead: a winter party left about 7 a.m., reached the summit around 1 p.m. and was back after dark, about 12 hours and roughly 10 miles and 5,000 ft car to car. The line has also been skied as part of a multi-day traverse of the whole range.

ops.value: A snow line: done in winter (a January ascent on hard snow) and in mid-May (a ski descent in spring snowpack). Not a summer rock route.

results.summary: Rename this to Standard Route: its content is the 1961 first-ascent line from the col west of the summit onto the north and northwest side, which no source calls a Southeast Route, and lower its grade from the unsupported Grade IV 5.8 to class 4-5.
results.evidence: The 1961 first-ascent account (September 8, 1961; Cooper, Denny, Whitmore and the Fireys) reached the west notch, which is the Himmel-Otto col, and followed a ledge onto the north face to find a class IV route. The peak's area page describes the standard way up as the narrow gully to the Himmel-Otto col, and an encyclopedia entry gives the easiest route as YDS class 5. No source found names a Southeast Route on Himmelhorn or grades any line on it Grade IV 5.8; the other documented lines, Wild Hair Crack (5.7) and Stonehenge (5.10-), are separate sibling rows. The row's own aspect, face, approach, beta, detailed rack and climbing section already describe a northwest-side line of class 4 to low 5th. The name, the 'Southeast Route' mentions in the day plan, timing, summit pin note and climbing section, the grade (both read sources are below 5.8, one class 4 and one class 5, so 'Class 4-5'), and the rappel prose (the '2' and the false-summit-notch descent belong to Wild Hair Crack) are changed. Not changed for want of sources: alpine_grade D+, commitment IV, gain/loss and distances, the Oct season end.
